content: Invasive bacterial pathogens are microorganisms capable of invading sterile areas of the body, such as the bloodstream, soft tissues (e.g., muscle or fat), and the meninges, which are the protective membranes surrounding the brain and spinal cord. These infections are particularly severe and can lead to life-threatening conditions. Four primary bacterial agents are responsible for severe invasive infections in children older than one month: Neisseria meningitidis (meningococcus), Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumococcus), Haemophilus influenzae, and Streptococcus agalactiae (Group B Streptococcus or GBS). Collectively, these pathogens account for more than half of the global deaths caused by meningitis. While meningitis can affect individuals of all ages, certain populations are at higher risk. For example, newborns are particularly vulnerable to GBS, young children are at increased risk of infections caused by meningococcus, pneumococcus, and H. influenzae, adolescents and young adults are more susceptible to meningococcal disease, and the elderly are at heightened risk of pneumococcal disease. Surveillance of invasive bacterial vaccine-preventable diseases (IB-VPD) plays a critical role in achieving the global goal of Defeating Meningitis by 2030. To standardize the monitoring of the global burden and etiology of IB-VPD, the World Health Organization (WHO) has been coordinating a global IB-VPD surveillance network since 2009. Objectives of IB-VPD Surveillance: 1. Quantify Disease Burden and Epidemiology: This includes tracking disease trends over time. 2. Evaluate Vaccine Impact: Assess how vaccines influence disease burden and epidemiology. 3. Characterize Circulating Serotypes/Serogroups: Generate evidence to guide the selection of appropriate vaccines. 4. Identify Gaps in Immunization Programs: Provide data to inform potential changes in vaccine policies. 5. Monitor Antimicrobial Resistance (AMR): Guide treatment decisions and improve healthcare outcomes. 6. Detect and Respond to Cases, Clusters, and Outbreaks: Enable rapid public health responses. 7. Identify At-Risk Populations and Geographic Areas: Implement and adapt control measures accordingly. Surveillance Approaches: Surveillance for IB-VPD requires skilled healthcare personnel to perform procedures such as lumbar punctures and blood collection for culture, while minimizing specimen contamination. Specimens must be transported promptly to high-quality laboratories to ensure accurate pathogen identification. Sentinel sites should be strategically chosen to attract a high volume of patients with the target diseases. Special Considerations: Surveillance is not pathogen-specific and includes N. meningitidis, S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, and GBS. Laboratory capacity is essential for identifying these organisms. Surveillance can be nationwide or regional and is typically aggregate passive surveillance. However, in the event of a meningitis outbreak caused by N. meningitidis, a rapid public health response, including reactive vaccination, is warranted. Mass gatherings have been associated with meningococcal disease outbreaks, and such cases must be reported under International Health Regulations (IHR). Surveillance for GBS is particularly challenging, as it is virtually nonexistent in many countries. Quantifying the burden of neonatal GBS disease is difficult, even in high-income countries, and is further complicated in lowand middle-income countries due to factors such as out-of-hospital births, early discharge of facility-born infants, limited care-seeking behavior, and lack of diagnostic resources. Specimen Collection and Laboratory Testing: Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF): For suspected meningitis cases, lumbar puncture should be performed to collect CSF before administering antibiotics. Ideally, 3 mL of CSF should be collected and divided into three tubes for chemical analysis, microbiological testing, and overall appearance assessment. If only one tube is available, it should be prioritized for microbiological testing. Blood: For culture, 1–3 mL of blood is adequate for children, while 5–10 mL is recommended for adults. Blood should be diluted in culture broth in the appropriate ratio to optimize bacterial growth, following the manufacturer’s recommendations. Specimen Storage and Transport: CSF specimens should be sent to the laboratory immediately and processed within two hours of collection. If transport is delayed, specimens can be inoculated into trans-isolate (T-I) medium and incubated at 35–37°C with 5% CO₂ until transport (up to four days). Specimens should not be refrigerated but stored at room temperature. Long-term storage of isolates should ideally be at -70°C. If this is not possible, -20°C storage is acceptable for further testing, such as serotyping and antimicrobial susceptibility testing. Public Health Response: Rapid detection and response to cases, clusters, and outbreaks are essential. Reactive vaccination and chemoprophylaxis may be required during outbreaks. Data from surveillance should be used to inform decision-making, evaluate vaccine impact, and guide public health interventions. This comprehensive approach to IB-VPD surveillance ensures timely detection, effective response, and informed decision-making to reduce the burden of these life-threatening diseases.
